fireworks.why: Red, gold and green bursts with spark rays tear through curling smoke in every frame, so it shows the colour range and the real fluid at once.

clumsy.why: The crowd scrambles and lands badly and the floor line visibly tips under them, which is the funniest and most characterful moment, though all rows of this widget look much alike.

gust.why: Every frame has strong brass wedges in changing directions, building to a full blast that fills the picture, while other rows go nearly empty between gusts.

duet.why: The two masses lie together along a seam and are then thrown apart with a spatter, so one clip shows both the attraction and the repulsion that define the widget.

vine.why: A dense, well-spread network of curling stems visibly thickens from frame to frame with bright growing tips, although the lines are thin at this size.

royal.why: The court is at its fullest and the stroke flicks and sends the marks streaking away, the one row that clearly shows the widget's dismissal.

comfort.why: A warm blush blooms and fades over the orange and pink fields in a rich composition, the clearest visible change of any row in this very gentle widget.

honey.why: The largest, most elegant span of sagging threads and heavy shapes fills the frame, and a new blob is pushed out partway through, though the movement is slow.

lazy.why: The clearest shapes of any row, and a mass on the right slowly heaves up and curls, the best of a widget that barely moves in any candidate, so the change stays small.

timeslice.why: A huge cut-up sphere of black and cream staircases holds the centre of the Riley stripes in every frame and keeps shifting, which shows the slit-scan shearing at its boldest.

fold.why: The mirrored colonies read clearly as twins, and the picture moves through saturated yellow, blue and pale red with strong, graphic shapes.

stella.why: Thick concentric frames pile up and thin out around a lively, balanced score with bold discs and an open centre, so the stripe idea is obvious; the widget stays restrained on every song, but this row shows it best.

fischinger.why: Bright discs, rings and bars snap from a scatter to a row, a full ring and an arch, so the figures each chord chooses are clear and the colour glows on the blue.

mclaren.why: This is the most saturated and varied weave, with neon cards in green, pink, cyan and orange streaming down at different widths and depths.

lenlye.why: The film is full edge to edge with thick wriggling pillars, zigzags, coils and a jagged star burst, so every kind of scratch boils at once without long black gaps.

klee.why: Every glaze from yellow-green through pink and orange to blue and red is present in a full mosaic, and the rows visibly climb and fall with bright pops of tile.

miro.why: This is the largest and richest composition, with big black blobs, checkered crescents where colours flip, and a blue cluster that grows while the line wanders through it.

delaunay.why: All three discs are fully lit in rich teal, violet, ochre and coral, and the colours change from frame to frame, unlike the rows where the big bass disc sits dim.

lewitt.why: The whole wall fills with crossing red, blue, gold and black lines that visibly thicken frame by frame, which shows the piling-up of systematic rules better than any other row.

ridges.why: This is the brightest and boldest stack, with a glowing front line that changes shape strongly from an arch to sharp peaks while the older lines roll back behind it.

matisse.why: Big saturated cut-outs crowd the wall and the ground flips from orange to deep green, so it is the richest colour and the clearest sign of chords rearranging the paper.

kusama.why: Huge dot colonies swarm over a dense net while the colours flood between blue and gold, so it is both the fullest composition and the most dramatic change.

ikeda.why: Dense barcodes and full-height strobes hit in every frame with streaming data rows around them, and it avoids the full white flashes that wash out other rows.

horizon.why: All rows are nearly still by design, but this one has the strongest glow on the horizon, a visible shift from warm grey to cool and the line itself moving, so it reads best as moving.

harmonograph.why: The line burns thick and gold in bright knots and melts between clearly different large figures, which shows off the one unbroken line far better than the thinner, dimmer rows.

kline.why: Massive cream bars fill the frame and each new strike visibly knocks the composition into a new shape, with the broken brush line threading between them.

score.why: This is the densest and most graphic page, with heavy beams and stemmed chords, and it builds to a black bass disc and a large circle, so it shows the score's full vocabulary.

boogie.why: This row (frames 1:39-1:45) has the busiest traffic and the biggest blocks, with large blue, red and grey crossings stacked along the lanes, so it reads most like Broadway Boogie Woogie, though the sheet's rows run together and the call is less certain than the others.

cells.why: Every frame (2:51-2:57) is a dense jewel-like mosaic in purple, blue, rust and rose with bright kernels, and the cells rearrange clearly from one frame to the next.

nebula.why: This is the only row where the grains form a large golden spiral that turns into pink and amber knots joined by threads (frames 9:03-9:09), while the other rows are mostly small scattered dots.

pixelsort.why: The melts are at their most visible here (frames 3:11-3:17), with wide sheets tearing across blue, red and yellow Kusama dots, so both the sort and the beauty of what it melts are obvious.

mandala.why: In six seconds (frames 2:35-2:41) it goes from white attack rays to an orange petal ring to a pink lace ring to a full peach bloom, showing everything the widget does.

martin.why: The widget is pale and slow on every row, but here (frames 1:03-1:09) the rose and blue bands deepen the most under the pencil grid, and the longer length gives that quiet change time to read.

murmuration.why: The flock passes through its whole vocabulary (frames 1:47-1:53), from red jittery shards to a melody ribbon to a bright cream lens to a sharp chord figure, and each frame is a clear shape.

marbling.why: This row (frames 3:55-4:01) has the widest ink range, cream through crimson to near-black, in large fine concentric bands that fill the frame and end up pushed and combed out of shape.

kandinsky.why: All the elements appear at once (frames 9:51-9:57), with a flurry of yellow triangles flying out around blue circles, red bars and thin constellation lines, filling the frame far better than the sparser rows.

rorschach.why: The whole mirrored blot sits clear on black and grows from a crisp, detailed form into a wider soaked one, so it reads as a real inkblot while it changes, though the ink is dark in every row.

squares.why: This row has the largest and brightest squares, spread across the frame and landing in heavy clusters, while the other songs leave them smaller or nearly gone.

flee.why: The hot shapes keep bolting into white-gold streaks across the frame, with small stragglers trembling beside them, so it stays dense and frantic without going empty.

current.why: This is the richest row by far, with big pours of pink and red dye curling around the white-gold thread, and the water visibly moving them.

strings.why: Several curved threads weave one legible band with bright knots and kinks running along it, full and changing without tipping into the tangle of the denser rows.

fields.why: The fields travel from maroon, purple and blue to blazing orange and red, which gives the biggest and most glowing colour change of any row.

brush.why: A red arc and a few slashes build into a dense calligraphic knot under two bone-white melody strokes, so you watch a balanced painting being written.

blocks.why: The torn slices stay full and bright in every frame, with white and red bars shifting across a wide band, though all the rows leave the top and bottom of the picture dark.

riley.why: Huge bass lenses swell out of the stripes, with chevron kinks and inverted bands cut through them, then fall back into a smaller lens, which is the strongest op-art moment here.

halftone.why: Every frame is full, with the red and pale dot screens overprinting in big overlapping rings that keep regrouping, so it shows the two-screen idea better than any other row.

fifths.why: The star blooms to fill the whole circle in dense spiky pink, then folds through white into pale blue, which makes it the richest shape with the clearest change.

suprematism.why: It starts as a few black bars and piles up into huge tilted red, cream and ochre slabs that fill the frame, the loud pile-up the widget is built for, and the slab scale beats every other row.

contours.why: Large warm hills and cool pits sit together in dense, finely drawn rings and reshape in each frame, so both colours and the mirrored map read clearly.

tunnel.why: Glowing ember walls fill the frame while the outlines shift between rings, squares and triangles, so it has the strongest sense of depth and speed.

scribble.why: Open loops, coils and red scratches build toward a dense central knot with struck strokes, showing all of the pen's vocabulary while the sheet visibly fills up.

pointillism.why: It has the widest spread of colour, from magenta through red and orange to yellow-green, in big soft fields of dots that shift steadily and fill the frame more than the other rows.

casket.why: All rows are poor because the sheet rendered casket with nothing under it, so it is almost entirely black; this is the best of them, with falling drips and the one visible long slash, but the widget melts what lies beneath and the clip should be rendered over a base widget to show that.
